concepts.title: GST, FinalPrice and EMI Computation
concepts.definition: A showroom query can chain arithmetic inside SELECT: add tax at 12 percent of the listed price to build the final price, then split that amount into ten equal monthly installments rounded down to a multiple of ten thousand, leaving the leftover payable at once. The MOD-style remainder isolates the leftover, and integer division by the installment count gives the clean EMI.
concepts.key_idea: Tax first, total second, remainder third: the leftover after stripping the last ten-thousands, divided by ten, is the payable EMI.
concepts.textbook_ref: leip101.txt Example 1.1, GST and EMI queries (lines 243-346)
question_patterns: calculate the GST at 12 percent of the price of car D001 costing 582613 and round it to one decimal place

for the car priced 673112, compute the GST, FinalPrice and EMI in multiples of 10000

solution_steps.explain: 12 percent of the listed price: 582613 * 12 / 100 = 69913.56

solution_steps.action: strip the leftover and split into ten
solution_steps.explain: removing the remainder on division by 10000 leaves 650000, and a tenth of it is the EMI 65000

concepts.title: String Functions: LEFT, RIGHT, INSTR, LENGTH, TRIM
concepts.definition: String functions dissect text values: LENGTH counts characters, INSTR reports where a substring first sits (0 when absent), LEFT and RIGHT copy characters from either end, MID/SUBSTR cut from a position onward, and LTRIM, RTRIM, TRIM shave padding spaces from the left, right or both sides. Combining INSTR with LEFT, for example, slices an email into its name part before the at-sign.
concepts.key_idea: Position functions locate, cut functions extract, and trimming functions subtract the padding from the raw length.

concepts.title: Date Functions: YEAR, MONTH, DAY, DAYNAME
concepts.definition: Date functions pick a stored date apart: YEAR, MONTH and DAY return the numeric parts, MONTHNAME and DAYNAME return words like November or Thursday, NOW() reads the clock, and DATE() keeps just the date part of a timestamp. Duration questions, such as months of service between two dates, reduce to counting month numbers on both ends and subtracting.
concepts.key_idea: Convert each date to a single month counter (year times twelve plus month); the difference is the span in months.

concepts.title: Aggregate Functions: MAX, MIN, AVG, SUM, COUNT
concepts.definition: Aggregate (multiple row) functions collapse a whole column of rows into one number: MAX and MIN take the extremes, SUM totals, AVG divides the total by the value count, COUNT counts non-null entries and COUNT(*) counts every row. On the chapter's INVENTORY table, the eight car prices give a total of 4608733 and an average of 576091.625.
concepts.key_idea: Sum the column once, divide by the row count for the average; extremes come from MAX and MIN without sorting.

concepts.title: GROUP BY and HAVING Clauses
concepts.definition: GROUP BY collects the rows sharing a value in one column into buckets so aggregates run per bucket, for instance the number of cars each customer bought. HAVING then filters those buckets after aggregation, keeping only the groups that pass a condition such as more than one purchase; WHERE cannot do this job because it filters rows before grouping.
concepts.key_idea: WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY buckets them, HAVING filters the buckets; per-group aggregates follow the same sum-then-divide arithmetic.

concepts.title: Set Operations: UNION, INTERSECT, MINUS
concepts.definition: Two relations with matching columns can be merged set-wise: UNION stacks the rows of both tables but shows a shared row once, INTERSECT keeps only rows present in both, and MINUS keeps rows of the first table absent from the second. Row counting follows the inclusion-exclusion arithmetic of sets.
concepts.key_idea: Subtract the overlap to get each table's exclusive rows; the union is the two exclusives plus one copy of the overlap.
question_patterns: how many rows does DANCE UNION MUSIC contain for the two event tables of the chapter

solution_steps.explain: 4 dance rows minus the 2 shared rows leave 2 dance-only participants

solution_steps.action: count the second table's exclusive rows
solution_steps.explain: 5 music rows minus the 2 shared rows leave 3 music-only participants
2 exclusives plus 3 exclusives plus 1 copy of the 2 shared rows gives 7 union rows

concepts.title: Cartesian Product Degree and Cardinality
concepts.definition: The Cartesian product pairs every row of one relation with every row of another. Its degree adds the two degrees (columns pile up side by side) and its cardinality multiplies the two cardinalities (each row of the first meets each row of the second); DANCE with MUSIC therefore yields degree 6 and cardinality 20.
concepts.key_idea: Columns add, rows multiply: the product relation's size is the product of the input sizes.
question_patterns: what are the degree and cardinality of DANCE X MUSIC

solution_steps.explain: 3 columns from each side line up into 3 + 3 = 6 columns
every one of the 4 rows pairs with every one of the 5 rows, giving 20 combinations

worked_examples.q: DANCE has 4 rows and MUSIC has 5. How many rows does their cartesian product hold?

concepts.title: JOIN and NATURAL JOIN on Two Tables
concepts.definition: A JOIN pulls related rows out of two tables by testing a condition, usually equality between a primary key and its foreign key; the condition may sit in WHERE, in JOIN ... ON, or be left implicit in NATURAL JOIN, which additionally drops the duplicated common column. Joining N tables on equality needs N-1 joins.
concepts.key_idea: JOIN filters the cartesian product down to matching pairs; NATURAL JOIN hides the repeated common column.

solution_steps.explain: one side's primary key matches the other side's foreign key on the shared attribute

concepts.title: Single Row versus Aggregate Functions
concepts.definition: Single row (scalar) functions such as POWER, ROUND, MOD, UPPER, LOWER and the date extractors work on one value per row and return one result per row, so they may appear in SELECT, WHERE or ORDER BY. Aggregate functions instead swallow a whole group of rows and return one value per group, and they live only in the SELECT list.
concepts.key_idea: Row functions transform each row independently; aggregates collapse many rows into a single figure.
question_patterns: state two differences between single row functions and aggregate functions

solution_steps.explain: scalar functions take one value; aggregates take a whole column of values
a scalar function answers per row; an aggregate answers once per group
scalar functions work in SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY; aggregates only in the SELECT list (or HAVING over groups)

worked_examples.q: POWER and UPPER return one result per row. Are they single-row or aggregate functions?
